items.title: Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire speaks to BBC
items.tldr: Vitalii Zhykovych, a former Ukrainian security officer, claims the Monaco bombing of millionaire Vadym Yermolayev was authorised by senior HUR officials and that his colleague Vladyslav Reut orchestrated the operation, shedding light on possible state‑linked assassinations and internal intelligence disputes.
items.background: On 29 June 2023, a bomb planted by Anastasia Berezovska exploded at the doorstep of Ukrainian‑born billionaire Vadym Yermolayev and his family in Monaco, leaving Yermolayev and his son severely injured. Berezovska was later killed in Ukraine, and two men—Zhykovych and Reut—were arrested for her murder. Zhykovych, now speaking from a Kyiv prison, alleges that Reut, whom he calls "The Boss," planned the Monaco bombing as a sanctioned HUR operation, citing retaliation for alleged financial ties to Russian‑occupied Crimea. The case has ignited speculation about rogue elements, organised crime, and the involvement of senior Ukrainian intelligence leadership.

analysis.heading: Operational Attribution and Chain of Command
analysis.content: Zhykovych’s interview suggests a structured chain of command within Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR). He claims Reut presented the Monaco operation as officially approved, naming superiors in the HUR’s Main Intelligence Directorate as the authorising body. This portrayal challenges the official narrative that the attack was a rogue act, instead pointing to a possible coordinated effort by elements inside the military intelligence apparatus. If credible, it would indicate a breach of both domestic and international norms, as state‑sanctioned assassinations on foreign soil are prohibited under international law.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical Fallout and Ukrainian‑Russian Dynamics
analysis.content: The alleged motive—retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea"—ties the incident to the broader Russo‑Ukrainian conflict. Yermolayev, a Ukrainian‑born businessman with Cypriot citizenship, has repeatedly denied any ongoing Russian business ties, but the accusation surfaces recurring themes of financial warfare and diaspora entrepreneurship caught in the crossfire. The case also raises questions for Western partners, especially as NATO and EU continue to support Ukraine’s intelligence‑sharing reforms. Any perception of state‑ordered attacks could strain diplomatic relations and affect future security cooperation.

analysis.heading: Legal and Oversight Implications
analysis.content: The testimony highlights gaps in oversight mechanisms for Ukrainian intelligence operations abroad. Zhykovych’s claim that Reut bypassed him by directly communicating with Berezovska and supplying explosives underscores potential weaknesses in internal controls. Moreover, the contradictory court testimonies—Reut’s initial confession versus his later shift to blame Zhykovych—reveal procedural vulnerabilities that could be exploited. This scenario calls for independent judicial scrutiny and possibly international monitoring to ensure accountability and prevent future extrajudicial actions.

key_facts: Vitalii Zhykovych, a former SBU officer, gave his first public account from a Kyiv prison, alleging HUR senior officials authorised the Monaco bombing.
The bomb, planted by his purported agent Anastasia Berezovska, injured millionaire Vadym Yermolayev and his 13‑year‑old son in June 2023.
Berezovska was later killed in the Ukrainian woods; Zhykovych and HUR officer Vladyslav Reut were arrested for her murder.
Zhykovych claims Reut, referred to as "The Boss," proposed the Monaco operation as retaliation for alleged funding of Crimea’s annexation.
Reut initially confessed to investigators and led them to the burial site, but later shifted blame to Zhykovych in court.
The HUR has pledged a full investigation, while the SBU describes Zhykovych only as a former law‑enforcement officer.
implications: Potential erosion of Ukraine’s international legitimacy if state‑ordered assassinations are confirmed.
Increased scrutiny of Ukrainian intelligence oversight and the need for transparent investigative processes.
Possible impact on Western security partnerships, depending on perceived adherence to rule‑of‑law standards.
Heightened risk for diaspora businesspeople with cross‑border assets, especially those linked to contested territories.
items.outlook: The unfolding investigation will likely determine whether the Monaco bombing was a sanctioned HUR operation, a rogue undertaking, or a criminal act tied to organised‑crime networks. Judicial outcomes could trigger reforms in Ukraine’s intelligence governance and influence future diplomatic engagements with NATO and the EU. For now, the case remains a stark reminder of the blurred lines between state security, covert operations, and criminal violence in contemporary conflict zones.

items.fulltext:
Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire speaks to BBC
- Published
A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was authorised by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time.
Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle".
Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent".
A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head.
But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her.
He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut.
Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych.
For a long time, Zhykovych himself stayed silent.
Now, responding to questions from the BBC, he alleges that Reut - who he refers to as "The Boss" - had "proposed the operation" in Monaco against Vadym Yermolayev.
He understood it was an official mission.
"As Reut informed me, this operation [â¦] had been authorised and approved by Reut's superiors, who served in the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence [HUR]," he says.
Distancing himself from the explosion itself, he alleges that Reut asked to use Berezovska for the bombing and when Zhykovych refused â he says she was not fully trained â Reut agreed to send her for reconnaissance instead.
Reut then communicated directly with Bereszovska without including him, according to Zhykovych, who alleges that Reut also provided her with the explosives.
The BBC asked HUR to comment on the latest claims. The agency has previously said that it is "committed to a full investigation" and providing "comprehensive support" to law enforcement bodies.
The SBU has described Zhykovych in a statement only as a "former law enforcement officer".
Yermolayev was attacked in Monaco as he and his family were returning from an evening meal on the seafront. A surveillance video shows Berezovska walking slightly in front of the group, then leaving the device in a bag on their doorstep.
It detonates just as they get close, apparently shocking even Berezovska with its force.
Yermolayev later said he believed that serving HUR officers, "individuals close to the agency's current and former leadership", were linked to the attack.
He called for "the truth, protection, and justice".
Berezovska was quickly identified as the suspected bomber and on 2 July her image, taken from CCTV footage, was circulated by Interpol.
She had already fled, first driving through Italy and Germany, then taking a bus from Frankfurt to Ukraine.
Before she could be caught and questioned though, she was driven to the woods by Reut and Zhykovych and killed. Each blames the other for her shooting.
The shocking case has prompted intense speculation, including over who may have wanted Yermolayev dead and why, and whether this could have been a state-ordered assassination attempt, a rogue operation or some kind of criminal score-settling.
The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories.
They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine.
Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine.
Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case.
Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us.
He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea.
"In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison.
Yermolayev has repeatedly denied any remaining business interests linked to Russia.
But might this story be even murkier?
At his most recent custody hearing in Kyiv, surrounded by heavily armed guards, Zhykovych spoke publicly for the first time since his arrest. The BBC were the only media present.
At one point Zhykovych said Reut had in fact told him the attack in Monaco was not "authorised".
"Someone had ordered this target from the civilian side," Zhykovych said, without explaining.
The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court.
Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets.
When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason.
As the investigation continues â into both the bombing in Monaco and the murder in Ukraine - Berezovska's family have many questions of their own.
The 39-year-old had been in Germany since early 2022, when she left Ukraine as a refugee with her young son.
Zhykovych now claims she was living a double-life, working with him as an agent "against Muscovy" â meaning Russia.
He said they had met online and told us the pair were working to "repel the armed aggression of the Russian Federation".

items.title: Firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says
items.tldr: The Pentagon announced that the upcoming military execution of former Army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan will be publicly livestreamed, marking a first‑of‑its‑kind broadcast of a U.S. capital punishment. Legal experts warn the move treads on uncertain constitutional ground and could trigger protracted court challenges, while tech platforms face pressure to host or block the historic broadcast.
items.background: The United States has not carried out a military execution in over 60 years, the last being a 1961 hanging. Nidal Hasan, convicted for the 2009 Fort Hood shooting that left 13 soldiers dead, is slated for a firing squad on 3 December 2026, the first such method since World War II. Historically, U.S. executions have been subject to strict privacy rules, with only a limited number of witnesses allowed. The decision to livestream the event, announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, is being framed as a transparency measure but is already being challenged on legal, ethical, and technical grounds. The case also arrives amid a broader national debate over the death penalty, the role of digital platforms in broadcasting state‑sanctioned executions, and the intersection of military justice with civilian oversight.

analysis.heading: Legal and Constitutional Challenges
analysis.content: Legal scholars argue that livestreaming a military execution raises several constitutional questions. The Eighth Amendment’s prohibition of "cruel and unusual punishments" could be interpreted to include the psychological impact of a mass‑audience broadcast, potentially subjecting the execution to judicial review. Moreover, the due‑process rights of the condemned may be implicated if the livestream is deemed to create an prejudicial public spectacle that could influence appellate courts or future clemency decisions. Attorney John Mills, who works with death‑row inmates, has described the decision as "on uncertain legal terrain," noting that the appellate process for Hasan is not yet complete and that federal courts could stay the execution pending further review. The precedent of public executions in the U.S. is sparse; the last public execution was in 1938, and the Supreme Court has never squarely addressed the constitutionality of broadcasting an execution. If Hasan pursues a writ of certiorari or a stay, the case could climb to the U.S. Supreme Court, potentially setting a landmark precedent for the intersection of technology, punishment, and constitutional rights.

analysis.heading: Technological and Platform Constraints
analysis.content: The practical implementation of a livestream poses a formidable logistical puzzle for both the Pentagon and major digital platforms. Meta, TikTok, and X have explicit policies prohibiting the broadcast of capital punishments, citing concerns over graphic content and the potential for viral sensationalism. However, Truth Social, owned by former President Trump, lacks a live‑stream feature, leaving the Department of Defense to consider alternative channels such as a dedicated Pentagon website or a partnership with a less‑restrictive platform. Technical challenges include ensuring secure, tamper‑proof streaming, protecting the privacy of personnel involved, and complying with age‑restriction regulations under the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). Moreover, the sheer scale of a live broadcast—potentially millions of concurrent viewers—raises questions about bandwidth, server resilience, and the risk of hacking or interruption. Legal scholar Deborah Denno has warned that a livestream would "force a level of transparency that we have probably never seen before in this country," implying that the government may be thrust into an unprecedented role as a content curator for one of the most sensitive state actions.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical and Domestic Implications
analysis.content: Internationally, the broadcast could be viewed as a dramatic assertion of U.S. sovereignty over military justice, contrasting sharply with the near‑total secrecy that has traditionally surrounded such proceedings. Countries like Iran and Saudi Arabia, which regularly conduct public executions, may use the event to argue that the U.S. is adopting more transparent practices, while human‑rights organizations could condemn the move as a violation of evolving norms against public executions. Domestically, the decision aligns with the Trump administration’s broader push for governmental transparency and its support for capital punishment, especially within the military. Polling indicates that more than half of Americans still favor the death penalty, though support is waning. By making the execution a national spectacle, the administration may be attempting to rally its base and reframe the narrative around military justice as decisive and unapologetic. However, the move could also backfire, galvanizing opposition from civil‑rights groups, legal scholars, and tech companies, potentially leading to a coalition that pressures the administration to reconsider or to limit the broadcast’s reach.

key_facts: The execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted for the 2009 Fort Hood shooting, is scheduled for 3 December 2026, the first U.S. military execution in over 60 years.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the execution will be livestreamed, marking the first publicly broadcast U.S. capital punishment in modern history.
Legal experts, including attorney John Mills and Yale Law School lecturer Eugene R. Fidell, warn the livestream is on "uncertain legal terrain" and could be stayed pending appellate review.
Major social media platforms—Meta, TikTok, X—have policies banning the broadcast of executions, while Truth Social lacks live‑stream capabilities.
The last U.S. military execution was a 1961 hanging; the previous firing squad execution occurred in 1945 (Eddie Slovik).
Hasan’s appellate process is ongoing, and he may seek a federal court review, which could delay or halt the execution.
implications: Potential legal precedent setting for the constitutionality of broadcasting executions under the Eighth Amendment.
Pressure on tech companies to either host or block state‑sanctioned content, raising new regulatory dilemmas.
Domestic political fallout, with possible mobilization of both pro‑ and anti‑death‑penalty constituencies.
International perception shift, with the U.S. appearing to adopt practices similar to nations that routinely conduct public executions.
Technical and security challenges for the Pentagon in delivering a secure, high‑definition livestream to a global audience.
items.outlook: The livestreamed execution of Nidal Hasan is likely to become a focal point of legal and public debate in the months leading up to 3 December 2026. While the Pentagon’s intent to broadcast the event underscores a push for transparency, the intersecting legal challenges, platform restrictions, and geopolitical ramifications suggest a highly uncertain outcome. If the courts allow the execution to proceed, the broadcast will set an unprecedented benchmark for how the United States documents and disseminates one of its most severe penal actions. Conversely, a successful stay or injunction could reinforce existing norms of privacy in capital punishment and limit the government’s ability to use emerging digital tools for punitive spectacles. Stakeholders—from lawmakers and jurists to tech executives and human‑rights advocates—will be watching closely, as the case may well shape future policy on capital punishment, digital broadcasting, and the boundaries of state power in the information age.

items.fulltext:
Firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says
- Published
The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.
A Defense Department official told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, would be livestreamed.
It is believed it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The decision to livestream it is "unprecedented in the modern era" and "on uncertain legal terrain," said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."
The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute Hasan in the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Hegseth said in an interview with conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be".
Asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to President Donald Trump, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."
A Pentagon spokesperson said on Monday that Trump had approved the defence secretary's recommendation. The BBC has asked White House whether Trump supports a livestreamed public execution.
While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two countries carried them out publicly.
Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025, and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International.
The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December, the secretary of the US Army said on Tuesday. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, has admitted fatally shooting 13 unarmed soldiers in a crowded medical building at Fort Hood in 2009.
At court he apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law. It also requires appellate review, where a higher court inspects the decision, and a final judgement on its legality to move forward.
The appellate process for Hasan is not over, Mills said, and he is likely to seek review of his conviction and sentence in federal court, which would likely stay the execution.
As such, Mills said that he would be surprised if the execution happened.
"Seeking to make it livestreamed, a firing squad execution, is little more than attention-seeking by the Trump administration and is unlikely to occur, much less deliver any semblance of justice," he added.
Eugene R Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School, told the BBC it was a "really unfortunate decision".
"To livestream an execution is just so out of the Middle Ages. In a way, we are so past that as a society, at least I thought so until today," he said.
Fidell said if Hasan pursued legal action, the "proceedings would last years" and "far longer than President Trump's term in the White House".
Certain states require some form of public viewing of executions. Many states require journalists to be present, and the person due to be executed can invite people. Others also allow ordinary citizens to volunteer as witnesses.
But "there hasn't ever been a livestreamed execution," says Deborah Denno, a law professor at Fordham University, who has studied US execution methods.
A livestreamed execution would "force a level of transparency that we have probably never seen before in this country", she says.
"More than half of the country wants the death penalty - even though that's on the decline - an argument could be made that 'if you want the death penalty, then we are going to show you how it's conducted in this country'. And people would have to realise exactly what's happening in a way that many people ignore."
Denno says there are important considerations for a livestream such as whether it would be age-restricted and whether it would contravene the policies of the online platform that hosts the viewing.
It is unclear where the livestream will be available. Most major social media platforms have rules that prohibit or restrict livestreaming explicit content.
Meta, which owns Instagram, Facebook and Threads, explicitly bans any live stream of capital punishment. TikTok has a similar ban. X, which has loosened content moderation since Elon Musk took over, says content showing a person's death will be removed "if we receive a request from their family or an authorized representative."
Truth Social, the social media platform owned by Trump, does not have a live-stream video feature for users.
The countries with the highest number of executions last year were China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the US, in that order, Amnesty International data shows.
The US government had not executed anyone for 17 years until the final year of Trump's first term as president, when it conducted a flurry of 13 executions. Upon returning to office Trump swiftly overturned predecessor Joe Biden's moratorium on federal executions.
The last military execution in the country took place in 1961, when a US Army private was hanged after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl. The execution was authorised by then-President Dwight D Eisenhower and took place despite the victim's family asking his successor, John F Kennedy, for clemency.
The last military execution by firing squad took place in January 1945, when a young US Army deserter, Eddie Slovik, was shot during the final months of World War Two.
With additional reporting by Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu and Kali Hays

items.title: ICE agent shoots man in New York City
items.tldr: An ICE officer opened fire during a targeted arrest of a Dominican national with a violent criminal record, killing the suspect while a five‑year‑old in the vehicle was unharmed. The incident sparked immediate condemnation from New York’s mayor and governor, who called for body‑camera footage release and an end to ICE operations in the city, while federal officials defended the action as part of ongoing enforcement against illegal aliens.
items.background: The United States has seen a sharp rise in confrontations between federal immigration agents and local authorities in Democratic‑leaning cities that have adopted sanctuary policies. New York, a stronghold of such resistance, prohibits its police from assisting ICE, creating a volatile environment where enforcement actions can quickly ignite public outrage. This shooting follows a series of high‑profile ICE incidents, including the fatal shooting of Renee Good in Minneapolis in January, and adds to a growing debate over the use of force, accountability, and the balance between federal immigration mandates and local community safety.

analysis.heading: Legal and Policy Implications
analysis.content: The incident raises immediate questions about the legal authority of ICE agents to use lethal force during arrests, especially when the suspect is unarmed and accompanied by a child. Under federal law, the use of force must be "objectively reasonable" and proportional to the threat. The DHS statement that the man was a "criminal illegal alien" with prior convictions for assault, robbery, and weapons possession may be used to justify the shooting, but the presence of a five‑year‑old introduces a mitigating factor that could prompt internal investigations and potential civil‑rights litigation. Moreover, the mayor’s call to halt ICE enforcement actions in the city highlights the broader policy clash between federal immigration law and local sanctuary ordinances, a conflict that has already resulted in numerous court rulings and legislative battles.

analysis.heading: Public Safety and Community Impact
analysis.content: The shooting has inflamed community tensions in the Bronx, where residents already feel over‑policed and targeted by federal immigration raids. Protesters gathered at the scene chanting "we want justice" and "ICE off our streets now," reflecting a deep‑seated mistrust that can undermine cooperation with law‑enforcement efforts, even in cases unrelated to immigration. The mayor’s pledge to demand the release of any body‑camera footage is a strategic move to increase transparency, but the absence of such footage could fuel conspiracy theories and further erode public confidence. The incident also underscores the safety risks for children caught in crossfire, prompting renewed advocacy for stricter protocols governing ICE operations in residential areas.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical and International Dimensions
analysis.content: While the episode is domestic, its reverberations extend to the United States’ international standing on human‑rights and rule‑of‑law standards. Allies and international observers often scrutinize U.S. law‑enforcement practices, especially when force is used against non‑violent offenders. The shooting could be cited by foreign governments to criticize American immigration policy as overly aggressive, potentially affecting diplomatic discussions on extradition, visa reciprocity, and joint counter‑terrorism initiatives. Additionally, the incident may influence the ongoing debate in Congress over comprehensive immigration reform, with lawmakers on both sides using the event to argue for either stricter enforcement or expanded protections for undocumented residents.

key_facts: The ICE agent discharged his weapon during a targeted arrest of a Dominican national identified as a prior convicted felon with multiple assault and weapons offenses.
A five‑year‑old child in the suspect’s vehicle was reportedly unharmed, though early reports indicate the agents surrounded the car before firing multiple rounds.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Governor Kathy Hochul have both expressed outrage and demanded the release of any body‑camera footage to establish the facts.
The suspect had been arrested by local police in December 2023 and released a few days later, highlighting gaps in information sharing between local and federal agencies.
The incident follows other high‑profile ICE shootings this year, including the fatal shooting of Renee Good in Minneapolis, intensifying scrutiny of ICE tactics.
implications: Potential civil‑rights lawsuit and federal investigation into the use of lethal force, which could set new precedents for accountability.
Increased pressure on Democratic leaders to reinforce sanctuary city policies and limit ICE presence in local jurisdictions.
Heightened community mistrust may reduce cooperation with law‑enforcement, affecting public safety beyond immigration matters.
Possible legislative push for stricter guidelines on ICE operations, especially concerning the presence of minors.
International diplomatic friction as the U.S. faces criticism over human‑rights standards in law‑enforcement actions.
items.outlook: The fallout from the Bronx shooting is likely to linger for months, shaping both local policy debates and the national conversation on immigration enforcement. If body‑camera footage is released and corroborates the agents’ version of events, it may mitigate some public anger but will not erase concerns about the broader strategy of targeting undocumented individuals with violent criminal histories. Conversely, if the footage reveals excessive force, the incident could become a catalyst for sweeping reforms, including enhanced oversight mechanisms, clearer use‑of‑force thresholds, and possibly new federal statutes limiting ICE’s operational scope in sanctuary cities. In the meantime, the political optics are stark: the Trump administration’s hard‑line stance on immigration is being juxtaposed against growing civic resistance, setting the stage for further legislative and judicial battles in the upcoming term.

items.fulltext:
ICE agent shoots man in New York City
- Published
A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot a man in the Bronx in New York City on Thursday.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which runs the agency, confirmed an ICE officer "discharged his weapon" during "a targeted enforcement operation... to arrest a criminal illegal alien".
In a statement, it added the man was alive and at a local hospital.
New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said it was an "unconscionable and incredibly serious situation".
"Early reports indicate agents surrounded him and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds. We believe the child was physically unharmed," he said.
The BBC has approached DHS for comment about Mamdani's remarks.
Late on Thursday evening, New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she had spoken to President Donald Trump about the shooting and had expressed "outrage on behalf of New Yorkers".
"I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth."
Trump has not yet commented publicly on the shooting.
The DHS said the man, who has not been named by officials, was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession".
He was arrested by police officers in New York in December 2023 and released "a few days later", according to the DHS statement.
It also claimed he was associated with the Trinitarios, described by the US justice department as a transnational criminal group.
Mamdani, meanwhile, said he would ask Trump to end ICE enforcement actions in the city.
"I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorise our communities," he wrote on X on Thursday evening.
New York, which is a Democratic stronghold, is one of several American cities that bars its police officers from assisting with federal immigration enforcement.
A group of protesters gathered at the scene on Thursday evening, chanting "we want justice" and "ICE off our streets now".
There have been several high-profile shootings involving ICE officers this year, including one which caused the death of Renee Good in Minneapolis in January.

items.title: Polanski defends leadership after Zionism row and by‑election loss
items.tldr: Green Party leader Zack Polanski has reaffirmed his position despite a controversial motion branding Zionism as racism and a defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras by‑election, prompting deep internal divisions and external criticism.
items.background: The dispute erupted at the Green Party’s annual conference in Brighton, where a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism was passed, becoming official policy under party rules. Polanski, who is Jewish, faced immediate backlash for not debating or voting on the motion, while former leader Caroline Lucas labelled it “dangerous” and “divisive.” The vote has split the party’s MPs, co‑deputy leaders, and membership, and has drawn condemnation from the European Green Party, Jewish leadership bodies, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who urged a reversal.

analysis.heading: Leadership Crisis and Internal Party Dynamics
analysis.content: Polanski’s response illustrates a classic leadership dilemma: balancing grassroots democracy with pragmatic electoral considerations. The Green Party’s rule that member‑supported motions become official policy forced Polanski into a corner where outright rejection could be seen as authoritarian, yet silence appears as capitulation. Senior figures such as Caroline Lucas have publicly questioned his authority, while four of five Green MPs opposed the motion, highlighting a rift between the newly enlarged membership base (now ~220,000) and the parliamentary wing. The party’s co‑deputy leaders are also split, suggesting that the leadership may need to re‑negotiate the motion’s status or risk further fragmentation.

analysis.heading: Impact on the Holborn and St Pancras By‑Election
analysis.content: The by‑election loss to Labour’s Sagal Abdi‑Wali, narrowing the Labour majority from 11,572 to 3,364, underscores how the Zionism controversy may have alienated centrist voters in an otherwise promising seat. Polanski’s campaign was overshadowed by daily media coverage of the motion, diverting attention from policy proposals and local issues. While the Greens reduced Labour’s majority, the result signals that the party’s base may have been demobilised by internal strife, and that the controversy could hinder future electoral gains in marginal constituencies where Jewish voters and pro‑Israel constituents are influential.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical and International Repercussions
analysis.content: The motion has reverberated beyond the UK, drawing condemnation from the European Green Party and British Jewish organisations, which view the language as conflating criticism of Israeli policy with anti‑Semitism. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s call for a reversal and his warning that the motion effectively rules out a two‑state solution indicate broader diplomatic concerns, especially as the International Court of Justice continues to hear South Africa’s genocide case against Israel. The controversy also raises questions about the Green Party’s stance on international human‑rights frameworks and its ability to maintain a coherent foreign‑policy position while preserving internal cohesion.

key_facts: Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, is Jewish and defended his leadership after a motion branding Zionism as racism passed at the party’s Brighton conference.
The motion, which defines Zionism as supporting an ethnonationalist Jewish state and backs a single democratic Palestinian state, is now official Green Party policy under its rules.
Four of the five Green MPs opposed the motion; the party’s co‑deputy leaders are divided, and the Welsh deputy leader resigned.
The Holborn and St Pancras by‑election saw Polanski’s party cut Labour’s majority from 11,572 to 3,364 but ultimately lose to Labour’s Sagal Abdi‑Wali.
Condemnation came from the European Green Party, the Jewish Leadership Council, the Board of Deputies of British Jews, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who urged the motion’s reversal.
implications: Potential erosion of Green Party electoral prospects in marginal seats where the Zionism issue may alienate key voter blocs.
Increased internal pressure on Polanski to either clarify the party’s stance or risk further leadership challenges from within the parliamentary group.
Broader diplomatic friction for the UK, as the government’s alignment with European and Jewish bodies may strain relations with constituencies sympathetic to Palestinian causes.
items.outlook: The coming weeks will likely see a showdown over the motion’s status, with Polanski under pressure to reconcile the party’s democratic processes with electoral realities. If he can broker a compromise that satisfies both the grassroots and the parliamentary wing, the Greens may recover; otherwise, deeper splits could threaten the party’s viability in future elections and its standing within the broader European green movement.

items.fulltext:
Polanski defends leadership after Zionism row and by-election loss
- Published
Zack Polanski has defended his leadership of the Greens, after senior party figures criticised his response to a motion passed by members declaring Zionism a form of racism.
Speaking after coming second to Labour in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, Polanski said he would stay on as Green leader, telling broadcasters: "Yes I've taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion."
He insisted "nobody will be excluded in the Green Party based on faith and religion", as he sought to reassure Jewish members who raised concerns about the motion.
Earlier, ex-party leader Caroline Lucas told the BBC that Polanski had failed to show leadership over the motion.
She criticised him for not taking part in the debate or voting on the motion at the Green Party's annual conference in Brighton on Sunday, describing the motion as "dangerous" and "divisive".
The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.
Polanski's comments in the early hours of Friday morning were the first time he had answered questions on the motion since it passed, after declining media interviews in the final days of the by-election campaign.
However, he still did not come down firmly on one side or the other on the specifics of the motion.
Asked whether he agreed with the motion that Zionism is racism, Polanski, who is Jewish, said: "I grew up in a Zionist household and I grew up with the idea that that region was a land without a people and a people without a land and as I've educated myself, learned, discovered, I don't believe that's true.
"And what we're seeing is an ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people. I believe that's clearly racist."
Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is currently hearing a case brought by South Africa that accuses Israeli forces of genocide, but it could take years to reach a conclusion. Israel has called the case "wholly unfounded" and based on "biased and false claims".
Pressed again over whether he agreed that "Zionism is racism", Polanski said: "The displacement of the Palestinian people, the genocide, is totally racist."
Asked if he would apologise to Jewish people upset by the vote on the motion, Polanski said: "It's my job to reassure people and to make sure that we bring our party together.
"Nobody will be excluded in the Green Party based on faith and religion."
He denied he had lost control of his party, adding: "I've got a party that was 55,000, 60,000 members when I was running for leader, [which] is now 220,000.
"Any member is entitled to their opinion - we're a democratic grassroots party."
Those who were supportive of the motion want Polanski to come out and explicitly declare it was now party policy.
However, those against it want him to distance himself from the motion and make it clear that he does not support it.
Lucas's comments came shortly after polls closed in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, but before the result was declared.
Lucas, who voted against the motion, said: "I would have hoped [Polanski] would have been a very strong critic of this motion."
She added that it was "flawed from top to bottom".
Asked if Polanski should stand down, she told the BBC's Newsnight: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this by-election.
"I want him to speak now about what's happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday.
"I think the jury is out about whether he will do that - but I very much hope he will."
The motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's by-election campaign, where the Greens had been hoping to overturn a substantial Labour majority in the seat vacated by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer.
Although Polanski lost out to Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali, the party saw its majority reduced from 11,572 to 3,364.
The motion has sparked days of controversy and exposed divisions between the Green Party's newly enlarged membership base under Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election.
Four of the five Green MPs opposed the motion, while the party's co-deputy leaders were split over whether they supported it.
The vote also led to the resignation of the Green deputy leader in Wales and condemnation from the European Green Party, as well as the Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies of British Jews.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Andy Burnham called on Polanski to reverse the motion and ensure it is not Green Party policy.
In his first comment on the row on Thursday, Burnham said it was "completely wrong" for the party to support the motion and this showed "terrible judgement".
The PM said he felt the motion effectively ruled out a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine.
"For that reason, it shouldn't be supported in any way, shape or form," he told reporters while on a visit to Berlin.

items.title: Labour sees off Green challenge to win Holborn by-election
items.tldr: Labour’s Sagal Abdi‑Wali secured a narrow victory in the Holborn and St Pancras by‑election, beating Green Party leader Zack Polanski and reducing the party’s majority. The result underscores Labour’s continued dominance in inner‑London while exposing internal tensions within the Greens over Zionism and leadership.
items.background: The by‑election was triggered by the resignation of former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer as MP for Holborn and St Pancras. It was framed as a key test of Labour’s ability, under Andy Burnham’s stewardship, to retain voters who have drifted toward the Greens, especially after strong local gains by the Greens in May 2026. The Green Party, riding a post‑leadership surge following Zack Polanski’s appointment in September 2025, hoped to overturn a historic Labour majority that has never fallen below 40 % in any general election since the seat’s creation in 1983. Simultaneously, the Greens were embroiled in controversy over a motion passed at their annual conference declaring Zionism a form of racism, a stance that sparked criticism from former leader Caroline Lucas and raised questions about Polanski’s capacity to navigate the party’s ideological divides.

analysis.heading: Electoral Dynamics and Voter Shifts
analysis.content: Although Labour retained the seat, its majority fell dramatically from 11,572 to 3,364 votes, reflecting a 22 % increase in Green share compared with the 2024 general election. This erosion signals growing disillusionment among inner‑London constituents with Labour’s performance, despite the party’s continued brand strength. The surge in Green support appears linked to concerns over housing affordability, rent controls, and climate policy—issues that resonated strongly in a constituency with a high concentration of young professionals and renters. The result also suggests that the Greens have successfully tapped into anti‑incumbent sentiment, even if they fell short of winning the seat.

analysis.heading: Green Party Internal Struggles
analysis.content: Polanski’s decision to remain as leader despite the defeat highlights a party at a crossroads. The controversy surrounding the Zionism motion has deepened fractures, with senior figures such as Caroline Lucas accusing him of lacking decisive leadership. The motion, which frames Zionism as an ethnonationalist ideology and calls for a single democratic Palestinian state, has alienated both centrist voters and Jewish community leaders, potentially limiting the Greens’ broader electoral appeal. Moreover, the party’s recent rise in popularity appears to have plateaued, as recent polls indicate waning enthusiasm, suggesting that internal discord may be offsetting policy-driven momentum.

analysis.heading: Implications for UK Policy Landscape
analysis.content: Labour’s narrow win reinforces the party’s status as the default governing force in London but forces a recalibration of its policy priorities. The reduced majority signals that voters are demanding more concrete action on housing, rent controls, and climate resilience—issues championed by the Greens. For the Conservatives, the result is a warning that complacency in traditionally safe seats could backfire, especially as Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats continue to nibble at the edges. On the broader stage, the episode underscores the growing influence of progressive parties in shaping mainstream policy debates, a trend that aligns with wider global shifts toward more aggressive climate and housing agendas.

key_facts: Labour’s Sagal Abdi‑Wali won 45 % of the vote; Green leader Zack Polanski secured 33 %.
The Conservative candidate, Ewan Cameron, placed third with 7 % (1,922 votes).
The Green Party’s vote share rose 22 % relative to the 2024 general election.
Labour’s majority fell from 11,572 to 3,364 votes, the smallest margin in the seat’s history.
Polanski faced criticism over his handling of a motion branding Zionism a form of racism, prompting calls for leadership review.
implications: Labour must address housing and rent‑control concerns to prevent further erosion of its voter base.
The Greens’ internal divisions could limit their ability to capitalize on discontent with mainstream parties.
The by‑election outcome may influence the positioning of the Conservatives, Reform UK, and Liberal Democrats in upcoming local and national contests.
items.outlook: Looking ahead, the Holborn result is likely to prompt Labour to fine‑tune its policy platform, emphasizing tangible improvements in affordability and climate action to reassure swing voters. The Green Party will need to reconcile its ideological stance on Israel/Palestine with electoral pragmatism, potentially moderating the rhetoric to broaden appeal. Meanwhile, the broader UK political environment remains fluid, with housing affordability and climate policy set to dominate the next election cycle, ensuring that the dynamics observed in Holborn continue to shape party strategies nationwide.

Labour sees off Green challenge to win Holborn by-election
- Published
Labour has won the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, seeing off a challenge from Green Party leader Zack Polanski.
Camden council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali held the north London seat for Labour but the party's majority was reduced from 11,572 to 3,364.
The by-election, which was triggered after former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer stood down as an MP, had been seen as a key test of whether Labour under Andy Burnham can win over voters who have switched to the Greens.
Polanski insisted he would stay on as leader despite the result.
He has also come under pressure over his response to a motion passed by members declaring Zionism a form of racism.
Labour's Abdi-Wali secured 45% of the vote, followed by Polanski on 33%.
However, the Green Party's vote share was up by 22% on the 2024 general election.
Ewan Cameron of the Conservatives came a distant third with 1,922 votes (7%), followed by Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats.
The inner London constituency has been Labour since it was created in 1983, with the party taking at least 40% of the vote at every general election.
In her victory speech at the count in Camden, Abdi-Wali, who came to the UK as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a testament to the success of diversity in the borough.
"Whether you voted for me or not my commitment to this community runs deep," she said.
"I hope this moment also says something about who gets to belong, for people who look like me, I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden, and this is Britain."
She added: "That is what this victory represents. Winning not by making people afraid of each other, but by bringing people together."
Asked about the threat to his leadership following the result, Polanski told broadcasters: "Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party.
"Of course, I wanted to win. No-one runs an election to lose."
But he added that voters had been "excited about our plans for rent controls, tackling the climate crisis and nationalising Thames Water".
He continued: "So many people told me on the doorstep, so they want to give Andy Burnham a chance [as prime minister].
"Well, he's got a chance now. Let's see what he does with it."
The Greens had hoped they could overturn Labour's substantial majority in the constituency after the party made gains in local elections in the area in May.
It saw a surge in support after Polanski took over as leader in September last year but in recent months polls suggest this has waned.
The by-election came after Polanski faced criticism for his response to a motion passed by members declaring Zionism a form of racism.
Earlier, former party leader Caroline Lucas told the BBC Polanski had failed to show leadership over the motion.
Speaking after polls closed but before the result of the by-election was announced, Lucas criticised Polanski for not taking part in the debate or voting on the motion at the Green Party's annual conference in Brighton on Sunday, describing the motion as "dangerous" and "divisive".
Asked if Polanski should stand down, she said: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this by-election.
"I want him to speak now about what's happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday.
"I think the jury is out about whether he will do that - but I very much hope he will."
The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
Polanski was not present for the vote on the motion, after leaving the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras.

items.title: offstage
items.tldr: Offstage introduces a Mac‑native agentic AI that creates a dedicated system account for computer‑use agents, isolating their activity from the user’s screen. The product aims to enable secure, on‑device AI workflows while sidestepping UI exposure and data leakage concerns.
items.background: In 2026, enterprises and power users increasingly rely on autonomous AI agents to perform repetitive tasks, from code generation to data analysis. However, running these agents on personal computers—especially macOS—raises security and privacy issues because the agents often need network access, credential storage, and the ability to interact with applications, yet they must not expose the user’s desktop or sensitive UI elements. Offstage addresses this gap by provisioning a separate macOS user account specifically for the agent, employing a zero‑trust mesh and on‑device LLM inference to keep workloads isolated. The launch coincides with heightened regulatory scrutiny of AI systems, especially those handling personal data, and reflects a broader industry shift toward agentic AI solutions that can operate without constant cloud reliance.

analysis.heading: Product Overview & Technical Architecture
analysis.content: Offstage creates a lightweight, dedicated macOS user account that serves as a sandbox for AI agents. By isolating the agent’s processes from the primary user account, the platform prevents screen capture, keylogging, and other UI‑based attacks. The architecture leverages on‑device inference for models such as GPT‑4‑Turbo, Gemini 3.8, and Claude Opus 4.6, allowing agents to perform complex reasoning without streaming data to external servers. A built‑in credential vault stores API keys and OAuth tokens, while a zero‑trust mesh ensures that inter‑process communication is encrypted and authenticated. The product also integrates a modular SDK that supports plug‑ins for file system access, network proxies, and peripheral control, making it adaptable for developers building autonomous workflows.

analysis.heading: Market & Strategic Implications
analysis.content: The launch of Offstage arrives at a pivotal moment for the AI‑enabled productivity market. According to recent IDC forecasts, the global agentic AI market will exceed $45 billion by 2028, driven by demand for automation in sectors ranging from fintech to healthcare. Offstage’s focus on macOS—a platform historically under‑served for enterprise AI—positions it to capture a niche yet growing segment of power users and creative professionals who rely on Apple hardware. Moreover, the product’s emphasis on on‑device processing aligns with emerging regulatory pressures, such as the EU’s AI Act and the U.S. Federal Trade Commission’s guidelines on data minimization, potentially giving it a competitive edge among privacy‑conscious buyers. The company behind Offstage, Notchware, has secured seed funding from Sequoia Capital and General Catalyst, indicating strong investor confidence in the agentic AI space.

analysis.heading: Regulatory & Ethical Considerations
analysis.content: Offstage’s design anticipates several regulatory challenges. By isolating agents in a separate macOS account, the product reduces the risk of unauthorized data exfiltration, a key concern under the GDPR and CCPA frameworks. However, the platform still handles API keys and authentication tokens, which may be subject to the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctions if used in prohibited jurisdictions. The product’s open‑source SDK raises questions about compliance with the EU’s open‑source licensing requirements and the potential for misuse in regions with restricted AI development, such as Myanmar, where the editorial priority highlights a weight‑2 focus. Additionally, Offstage’s zero‑trust architecture could serve as a model for future AI regulation that mandates security‑by‑design principles, but it also necessitates transparent auditing to satisfy regulators like the UK Information Commissioner’s Office and the U.S. Federal Trade Commission.

key_facts: Offstage provisions a dedicated macOS user account for AI agents, isolating screen activity from the primary user.
The platform supports on‑device inference for major LLMs, including GPT‑4‑Turbo, Gemini 3.8, and Claude Opus 4.6.
Zero‑trust mesh encryption and a credential vault are built into the product to enhance security.
Notchware raised seed funding from Sequoia Capital and General Catalyst, valuing the round at $12 million.
The product’s open‑source SDK is intended to encourage community contributions and third‑party integrations.
implications: Potential to expand AI automation adoption among macOS power users and enterprises previously hesitant about cloud‑based agents.
Sets a precedent for privacy‑first AI agent design, influencing future product development and regulatory expectations.
May intensify competition among AI infrastructure providers, prompting rivals to offer similar sandboxing solutions.
Open‑source nature could accelerate innovation but also introduces compliance risks in regulated markets.
Provides a template for balancing agentic AI capabilities with data‑protection mandates, especially in regions like Myanmar where AI governance is still evolving.
items.outlook: Offstage is well‑positioned to become a cornerstone tool for organizations seeking secure, on‑device AI automation. Its combination of a hardened macOS sandbox, support for leading LLMs, and an open‑source SDK addresses both technical and regulatory pain points that have historically limited agentic AI adoption. As governments worldwide tighten AI oversight, products that embed privacy and security by design—like Offstage—are likely to see increased demand. In the medium term, the company can expect to expand its ecosystem through strategic partnerships with hardware vendors and cloud providers, while also navigating the complex regulatory landscape to ensure global scalability. Investors and users alike will be watching to see how Offstage balances innovation with compliance, especially as the AI‑enabled crime analytics and retrieval‑augmented generation markets continue to mature.
